SSgt Danny K. Lewis of the 42nd Security Police Squadron first sighted the object at about 1945 on 27 October 1975 while on duty at the munitions storage area; Sgt Clifton W. Blakeslee and SSgt William J. Long saw a similar craft the following night; SSgt James P. Sampley of the 2192nd Communications Squadron tracked it on tower radar; and Sgt Grover K. Eggleston tracked it for forty minutes before it vanished from the screen.

Named Loring witnesses are in the contemporaneous record rather than in any interview programme: SSgt Danny K. Lewis, Sgt Clifton W. Blakeslee, SSgt William J. Long, SSgt Michael D. Scott, TSgt David E. Mott and Capt. Richard R. Fuhs of the 42nd Security Police Squadron; SSgt James P. Sampley and Sgt Grover K. Eggleston of the 2192nd Communications Squadron; Sgt Steven Eichner and Sgt R. Jones of a B-52 crew; and Col. Richard E. Chapman, Commander of the 42nd Bomb Wing, who implemented a Security Option 3 alert.

desc: NICAP is the civilian organisation the board narrates constantly and has never named as an entity. It was forming at 1536 Connecticut Avenue NW in October 1956 under Thomas Townsend Brown, who told a Scripps-Howard reporter he was executive vice chairman pro tempore and that the group would elect its nine-man board of governors on 1 November; the clipping is in the FBI's own file on the organisation. By 1964 it was directed by Maj. Donald E. Keyhoe with Richard H. Hall as acting director and editor, carried a former Director of Central Intelligence and a former Blue Book headquarters monitor on its board, and published The UFO Evidence, which it sent to every Member of Congress and which the CIA filed. It is the exact official-and-civilian boundary the board argues about: a private body, staffed at the top by people who had held the government's own positions, campaigning for the hearings the government did not hold. The District of Columbia corporate register itself was not opened, so the incorporation rests on NICAP's own statement of it.

dossier.denialPosture: NICAP issues no denials. It receives none either, in the sense the board means: the denial link on this node has no direction the record establishes. What is documented is the charge running from the civilian side, in print, addressed to Congress. The 1964 volume states that the Air Force 'has practiced an intolerable degree of secrecy keeping the public in the dark about the amount and possible significance of UFO evidence', and the same volume records that copies went to every Member of Congress. The board carries the accusation as published text and declines to convert it into a directed denial by the Air Force, because no Air Force response is in the record opened here.
dossier.narrative:
The board narrates this organisation constantly and had never named it as an entity until now, which is itself the argument for its presence. Nearly every legacy-era episode the board carries has a NICAP shape to it: a case pressed publicly by a civilian committee whose officers had held the government's own positions, against an Air Force programme that answered in press releases. The 1964 volume states the charge in print and says where it was sent: the Air Force 'has practiced an intolerable degree of secrecy keeping the public in the dark about the amount and possible significance of UFO evidence', and 'Copies of this report have been sent to all Members of Congress.' That is a civilian body performing an oversight function that Congress was not performing.

What makes the node structural rather than merely historical is the composition of the board of governors. A former Director of Central Intelligence sat on it for five years and joined the campaign for hearings. The former Air Force Headquarters monitor of Project Blue Book, the liaison officer between the Dayton project and the Pentagon, sat on it too. This board spends most of its length tracking people who moved between government programmes and private vehicles; NICAP is the earliest well-documented instance in the legacy era, and the direction of travel is out of the official effort and into public advocacy against it.

The surveillance runs the other way and is equally documented. The FBI opened file 100-35992 on the organisation and recorded its self-description as furnished by its secretary Richard H. Hall to a Special Agent of the Washington Field Office in May 1961. The copy of The UFO Evidence that this board reads is the CIA's own, released as CIA-RDP81R00560R000100010001-0. A civilian committee campaigning for hearings had a Bureau file and an Agency reading copy. Both facts come from the government's own paper.
openQuestions: The District of Columbia corporate register was not opened. The incorporation and its 1956 date rest on NICAP's own statement of them in the 1964 volume, and nothing independent confirms either.
The board holds no end date for the organisation and none for Keyhoe's directorship. The node runs open because nothing opened here closes it.

The custody of the NICAP case files rests on the National UFO Historical Records Center's own account of its collections, which is why that link is Tier 2. No inventory, deed of gift or transfer record has been seen.
dossier.whatItIs: The National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena, a civilian body at 1536 Connecticut Avenue NW in Washington DC. It states its own legal form and year: 'NICAP is a non-profit organization incorporated in the District of Columbia (1956).' It was forming in October 1956 under Thomas Townsend Brown, who told a Scripps-Howard reporter that he was executive vice chairman pro tempore and that the group would elect its nine-man board of governors on 1 November. By 1964 it was directed by Maj. Donald E. Keyhoe with Richard H. Hall as acting director and editor, and it published The UFO Evidence, sending copies to every Member of Congress.
dossier.whyImplicated: NICAP is the exact boundary this board argues about, staffed from the government side. A private organisation campaigning for hearings the government would not hold, whose board of governors carried a former Director of Central Intelligence and the former Air Force Headquarters monitor of Project Blue Book. Vice Admiral R. H. Hillenkoetter served five years on that board and in 1961 joined a majority of it in urging a Congressional investigation. Dewey Fournet Jr. had been the Pentagon's own liaison to the Dayton project. The organisation is not implicated in concealment; it is implicated in the structure, because it shows senior people moving from the inside of the official effort to the outside of it and then pressing the inside from there. The FBI kept a file on it and the CIA filed its book.

timeline.label: NICAP incorporated in the District of Columbia
timeline.text: The National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena states in its own 1964 volume that it is a non-profit organization incorporated in the District of Columbia in 1956. A Washington Daily News report of 23 October 1956, filed in the FBI's NICAP file, records the organisation forming at 1536 Connecticut Avenue NW under T. Townsend Brown of Leesburg, Virginia, executive vice chairman pro tempore, with a nine-man board of governors still to be elected on 1 November. The District's own corporate register was not opened.
